About: Pulling Your Arms In — Angular Momentum Held, Energy Not

Source

Topic
Rigid-body rotation — conservation of angular momentum
Simulation
Spinning skater on a frictionless turntable, pulling arms in and out
Concept
When there is no external torque, angular momentum L is conserved — but kinetic energy is not, because changing the moment of inertia requires work.
Serves
JEE / NCERT Class 11 rotational mechanics: L = Iω, KE = ½Iω² = L²/(2I), conservation laws distinguished from each other.
Inquiry
As the arms come in, what happens to L, and what happens to KE?
Misconception
"If angular momentum is conserved, energy must be too" — L and KE are different quantities with different formulas, and they behave differently.

Pulling Your Arms In

Guided Inquiry

1 · The setup

A skater spins on a frictionless turntable — nothing outside her body exerts a torque. She holds a weight in each hand, arms extended.

Beside her stand two bars: angular momentum L and kinetic energy KE. They start with her arms out. Next you will predict what those bars do when she pulls the weights in.

2 · Predict — before you pull

You are about to pull the arms in. What will the two bars do?

3 · Pull them in

Drag the Arm extension slider from the right (arms out) toward the left (arms in). Watch the two bars.

The L bar does not move by a pixel. The KE bar climbs. The skater spins visibly faster.

4 · Where did the energy come from?

Nothing outside the skater did anything. So the energy came from her. Pulling the weights inward, she is pulling them against their tendency to fly outward in a straight line — that inward pull, times the distance she moves them, is work. And that work is exactly the kinetic energy she gains.

Push the arms back OUT. The KE bar falls back down — she gets that work back as the weights push her arms outward. L stays flat the whole time.

5 · The rule

L = Iω is conserved when no external torque acts. KE = ½Iω² = L²/(2I) is not — because I itself changed, and changing I took work.

These are different quantities with different formulas. Conservation of one does not imply conservation of the other. Play with both sliders now — you own the sim.

01

At a glance

A skater spins on a frictionless turntable, holding a weight in each hand. You change how far the weights are from her axis. Two bars beside her track her angular momentum L and her kinetic energy KE.

What you'll learn

  • How a spinning body's moment of inertia depends on where its mass sits relative to the axis.
  • How angular momentum and kinetic energy are defined for a spinning body.
  • What happens to each when the body changes its shape while it spins.
Top view: trunk, two arms of length r, two weights, and the two bars (shown empty here).

What's on screen

  • Weights (orange): one on each arm. The arms turn with the turntable, and a label gives r.
  • Spin arrow (teal) around the trunk, with a label for ω, the spin rate.
  • Turntable: the dashed circle. It has no friction.
  • Two bars on the right: L (teal) with a dashed tick marking its starting value, and KE (orange), each with a number below.
See itStart with the arms fully out. Watch for: r = 1.00 m, ω = 2.00 rad/s, and the two bars at 8.00 kg·m²/s and 8.00 J.

Fixed: the trunk has I = 1.2 kg·m², each weight is 1.4 kg, and nothing outside the skater exerts a torque. The arms have no mass of their own.

03

Pulling the weights in lowers I = Itrunk + 2 m r²

The moment of inertia of the skater is the sum of two parts: the trunk, which is fixed, and the two weights, which count as point masses at distance r:

I = Itrunk + 2 m r²
Itrunk = 1.2 kg·m², m = 1.4 kg.

Distance counts squared, so I falls steeply as the weights come in. It cannot reach zero, because the trunk always stays:

rI
1.00 m4.00 kg·m²
0.50 m1.90 kg·m²
0.20 m1.31 kg·m²

Angular momentum and kinetic energy of a spinning body are defined by I and the spin rate ω: L = Iω and KE = ½Iω².

See itPull the weights in to r = 0.50 m. Watch for: the I readout falling from 4.00 to 1.90 kg·m².
04

With no external torque, L = Iω stays constant

Angular momentum changes only when an external torque acts. The turntable is frictionless and the skater pulls with internal forces only, so L is conserved while I changes. The spin rate must therefore adjust:

I1 ω1 = I2 ω2, so ω2 = ω1 I1 / I2

Starting at r = 1.00 m with ω₀ = 2.0 rad/s, L = 4.00 × 2.00 = 8.00 kg·m²/s:

rIωL
1.00 m4.002.00 rad/s8.00
0.50 m1.904.21 rad/s8.00
0.20 m1.316.10 rad/s8.00

L is in kg·m²/s and I in kg·m². The L bar does not move, while the spin visibly quickens.

See itPull the weights in to r = 0.50 m. Watch for: ω rising from 2.00 to 4.21 rad/s while L stays at 8.00.
05

KE = L²/(2I) rises when I falls

Kinetic energy can be written with L in place of ω:

KE = ½ I ω² = L² / (2I)

With L fixed, KE is inversely proportional to I. Halving I doubles KE. So kinetic energy is not conserved, even though angular momentum is. They are different quantities with different formulas.

rIKE
1.00 m4.00 kg·m²8.00 J
0.50 m1.90 kg·m²16.84 J
0.20 m1.31 kg·m²24.39 J

At fixed I, KE goes as ω², so doubling ω₀ quadruples it while L only doubles.

See itPull the weights in all the way, to r = 0.20 m. Watch for: KE climbing from 8.00 to 24.39 J while L stays at 8.00.
See itKeep the arms out and set ω₀ to 4.0 rad/s. Watch for: L doubling to 16.00 and KE rising four times to 32.00 J.
06

The extra energy is the work the skater does

Nothing outside the skater supplies the energy, so it comes from her. To keep a weight circling at radius r the arm must pull it inward with force m ω² r. Pulling the weight inward through dr does work on it:

ΔKE = Wskater = ∫ Fpull dr

Taking ω from L/I at each r, this integral over both weights equals the KE gain exactly: 8.84 J from r = 1.00 m to 0.50 m, and 16.39 J from 1.00 m to 0.20 m. Pushing the arms back out reverses it. The weights do work on her, and KE falls back while L stays put.

See itTake the weights in to r = 0.50 m. Watch for: KE reading 16.84 J, which is 8.84 J above the 8.00 J it had at r = 1.00 m.
07

Where it matters

  • Skaters. A skater pulls in her arms to spin faster and extends them to slow down. Her kinetic energy changes each time, paid for by her muscles.
  • Divers. A diver tucks to complete somersaults, then opens out before entering the water, which lowers the spin rate.
  • Collapsing stars. A star that shrinks to a much smaller radius spins faster. A pulsar is the extreme case.
  • Rotating platforms. A person who walks inward on a freely turning platform makes it spin faster. The same L = Iω bookkeeping applies.
08

Summary

In one line. A skater's moment of inertia depends on how far her weights are from the axis, and the sim follows what happens to L and KE as she changes that distance.

Key points

  • I = Itrunk + 2 m r². Pulling the weights in lowers I.
  • With no external torque, L = Iω is conserved, so ω rises as I falls.
  • KE = L²/(2I) rises as I falls. The extra energy is the skater's work.

Common mix-ups

  • "If L is conserved, KE must be conserved too." They are different quantities. Changing I changes KE at fixed L.
  • "Pulling the arms in adds angular momentum." It changes the spin rate, not L.
  • "The turntable pushes her faster." The turntable is frictionless and applies no torque. The energy comes from her arms.

Things to try on your own

  • Find the r at which ω is 5.00 rad/s when ω₀ = 2.0 rad/s at r = 1.00 m, then check it.
  • Set ω₀ = 3.0 rad/s with the arms in, and see how the L bar changes. Why does it?
  • Predict KE at r = 0.35 m, then read it from the bar.
